# Atrial Fibrillation: Diagnosis and Management

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia,
affecting approximately 33 million individuals worldwide. Its prevalence
increases with age, reaching approximately 10% in adults over 80 years. ## Pathophysiology

The hallmark of AF is chaotic, rapid atrial electrical activity resulting in
irregular ventricular response. Multiple re-entrant wavelets propagate
simultaneously through the atrial myocardium. Heart rate typically ranges from
100-160 bpm during untreated AF. Key pathological mechanisms include:
- Electrical remodelling: shortening of the atrial refractory period
- Structural remodelling: atrial fibrosis and dilation
- Autonomic modulation: sympathetic and parasympathetic triggers

## Diagnosis

Diagnosis is confirmed by 12-lead ECG showing irregularly irregular rhythm
with absence of distinct P waves.
title: Atrial Fibrillation: Diagnosis and Management

text:
The QRS complex is usually narrow (<120 ms)
unless aberrant conduction or bundle branch block exists. Diagnostic criteria:
- Irregular RR intervals with no distinct P waves
- Atrial rate 350-600 impulses per minute
- Ventricular rate typically 100-160 bpm (untreated)

Holter monitoring (24-48 hour ambulatory ECG) or implantable loop recorders
are used to detect paroxysmal AF when standard ECG is non-diagnostic.
title: Atrial Fibrillation: Diagnosis and Management

text:
## Risk Stratification

The CHA2DS2-VASc score guides anticoagulation decisions:
- C: Congestive heart failure (1 point)
- H: Hypertension (1 point)
- A2: Age >= 75 years (2 points)
- D: Diabetes mellitus (1 point)
- S2: Stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2 points)
- V: Vascular disease (1 point)
- A: Age 65-74 years (1 point)
- Sc: Sex category female (1 point)

Score >= 2 in males or >= 3 in females: anticoagulation strongly recommended. Bleeding risk is assessed with the HAS-BLED score. A high HAS-BLED score
(>= 3) should prompt correction of modifiable bleeding risk factors, not
withholding of anticoagulation. ## Treatment

### Rate Control

Rate control is the initial strategy in most patients. Target resting
heart rate is <110 bpm (lenient) or <80 bpm (strict, selected patients).
title: Atrial Fibrillation: Diagnosis and Management

text:
Target resting
heart rate is <110 bpm (lenient) or <80 bpm (strict, selected patients). Agents:
- Beta-blockers: metoprolol succinate 25-200 mg/day, bisoprolol 2.5-10 mg/day
- Non-dihydropyridine CCBs: diltiazem 120-360 mg/day, verapamil 120-480 mg/day
- Digoxin: 0.125-0.25 mg/day (primarily in sedentary patients with HFrEF)

### Rhythm Control

Rhythm control is preferred in symptomatic patients, younger patients, and
those with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF).
title: Atrial Fibrillation: Diagnosis and Management

text:
Antiarrhythmic drugs (AADs):
- Flecainide 100-200 mg BID (structurally normal heart only)
- Propafenone 150-300 mg TID (structurally normal heart only)
- Amiodarone 200 mg/day maintenance (most effective, most side effects)
- Dronedarone 400 mg BID (avoid in permanent AF or severe HF)

Catheter ablation (pulmonary vein isolation, PVI) achieves rhythm control
in 60-80% of patients at 1 year and is preferred over AADs in many centres.
title: Atrial Fibrillation: Diagnosis and Management

text:
### Anticoagulation

Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are preferred over warfarin:
- Apixaban 5 mg BID (or 2.5 mg BID if >= 2 of: age >= 80, weight <= 60 kg, creatinine >= 1.5 mg/dL)
- Rivaroxaban 20 mg OD with evening meal
- Dabigatran 150 mg BID (or 110 mg BID in selected patients)
- Edoxaban 60 mg OD (or 30 mg OD if CrCl 15-50 mL/min, weight <= 60 kg)

Warfarin (target INR 2.0-3.0) remains appropriate when DOACs are unavailable,
in patients with mechanical heart valves, or in moderate-to-severe mitral
stenosis.
title: Atrial Fibrillation: Diagnosis and Management

text:
## Prognosis

AF significantly increases the risk of:
- Stroke: 5-fold increase; 20-30% of all strokes are AF-related
- Heart failure: bidirectional relationship; AF precipitates and worsens HF
- Dementia: independent risk factor
- Mortality: 2-fold increase in age-adjusted mortality

With appropriate anticoagulation, stroke risk is reduced by 60-70%. Early rhythm control (initiated within 1 year of diagnosis) is associated
with improved cardiovascular outcomes in selected patients (EAST-AFNET 4 trial).
title: Atrial Fibrillation: Diagnosis and Management

# Heart Failure: Classification, Diagnosis, and Management

Heart failure (HF) is a clinical syndrome characterised by the heart's
inability to pump sufficient blood to meet the body's metabolic demands, or
doing so only at the expense of elevated filling pressures. It affects
approximately 64 million people globally and carries a 5-year mortality
rate exceeding 50%. ## Classification by Ejection Fraction

The 2021 ESC Guidelines classify HF by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF):

| Phenotype | LVEF | Abbreviation |
| Reduced | < 40% | HFrEF |
| Mildly reduced | 40-49% | HFmrEF |
| Preserved | >= 50% | HFpEF |

HFrEF accounts for approximately 50% of all HF cases. HFpEF is increasingly
prevalent, particularly in older women with hypertension, obesity, and
diabetes.
title: Heart Failure: Classification, Diagnosis, and Management

text:
HFpEF is increasingly
prevalent, particularly in older women with hypertension, obesity, and
diabetes. ## Aetiology

Common causes by phenotype:

HFrEF:
- Ischaemic cardiomyopathy (coronary artery disease): ~50% of cases
- Dilated cardiomyopathy (idiopathic, genetic, toxic: alcohol, chemotherapy)
- Myocarditis (viral, autoimmune)
- Valvular heart disease (aortic regurgitation, mitral regurgitation)

HFpEF:
- Hypertension (most common)
- Obesity and metabolic syndrome
- Atrial fibrillation
- Infiltrative disease (amyloidosis, haemochromatosis)

## Diagnosis

### Symptoms and Signs

Symptoms: dyspnoea (exertional, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea),
fatigue, ankle oedema, reduced exercise tolerance. Signs: elevated JVP, S3 gallop, bilateral basal crackles, peripheral oedema,
ascites, hepatomegaly.
title: Heart Failure: Classification, Diagnosis, and Management

text:
Signs: elevated JVP, S3 gallop, bilateral basal crackles, peripheral oedema,
ascites, hepatomegaly. ### Investigations

- ECG: may show LVH, bundle branch block, AF, Q waves (prior MI)
- Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly, pulmonary oedema (Kerley B lines, bat-wing pattern)
- Echocardiography: essential - LVEF, wall motion, valvular pathology, diastolic function
- BNP/NT-proBNP: BNP > 35 pg/mL or NT-proBNP > 125 pg/mL supports HF diagnosis
- Cardiac MRI: gold standard for myocardial characterisation

## Treatment

### Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy (GDMT) for HFrEF

The four pillars of GDMT reduce mortality and hospitalisation:

1. ACE inhibitors or ARBs (if ACE-I intolerant):
- Enalapril 2.5-20 mg BID, ramipril 2.5-10 mg/day
- Losartan 25-150 mg/day, candesartan 4-32 mg/day

2.
title: Heart Failure: Classification, Diagnosis, and Management

text:
Beta-blockers (only after clinical stability):
- Carvedilol 3.125-25 mg BID
- Metoprolol succinate 12.5-200 mg/day
- Bisoprolol 1.25-10 mg/day

3. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs):
- Spironolactone 25-50 mg/day
- Eplerenone 25-50 mg/day
- Monitor K+ and renal function closely (risk of hyperkalaemia)

4. SGLT2 inhibitors (mortality benefit independent of diabetes):
- Dapagliflozin 10 mg/day
- Empagliflozin 10 mg/day

ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan 24/26 - 97/103 mg BID) replaces ACE-I/ARB in
selected patients who remain symptomatic on optimised GDMT.
title: Heart Failure: Classification, Diagnosis, and Management

text:
### Device Therapy

- ICD: primary prevention in HFrEF with LVEF <= 35% on optimal GDMT
(at least 3 months after initiation) in patients with life expectancy > 1 year
- CRT-D: LBBB with QRS >= 150 ms and LVEF <= 35% and NYHA class II-III

### Decongestive Therapy

Loop diuretics (furosemide 20-500 mg/day) remain the cornerstone of
symptom management and are titrated to maintain euvolaemia. ## Monitoring and Follow-Up

- BNP/NT-proBNP guided therapy may help optimise GDMT
- Renal function, electrolytes, and BP every 1-2 weeks during up-titration
- 6-minute walk test and NYHA class reassessment at each visit
- Remote haemodynamic monitoring (CardioMEMS) reduces HF hospitalisation
in NYHA Class III patients

## Prognosis

One-year mortality is approximately 20-30% for hospitalised HF patients.
title: Heart Failure: Classification, Diagnosis, and Management

text:
The MAGGIC meta-analysis identified predictors of poor prognosis:
male sex, lower LVEF, lower systolic BP, higher NYHA class, lower BMI,
current smoking, diabetes, and renal impairment.
title: Heart Failure: Classification, Diagnosis, and Management

# Hypertension: Diagnosis and Treatment
Hypertension (HTN) affects more than 1.28 billion adults worldwide and is
the leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease (CVD),
stroke, and chronic kidney disease. Despite effective treatments, only
approximately 20% of hypertensive patients achieve adequate blood pressure
(BP) control globally. ## Definition and Classification
Blood pressure classification (ACC/AHA 2017 guidelines):
- Normal: systolic <120 mmHg and diastolic <80 mmHg
- Elevated: systolic 120-129 mmHg and diastolic <80 mmHg
- Stage 1 HTN: systolic 130-139 mmHg or diastolic 80-89 mmHg
- Stage 2 HTN: systolic >=140 mmHg or diastolic >=90 mmHg
- Hypertensive crisis: systolic >180 mmHg and/or diastolic >120 mmHg
ESC/ESH 2018 guidelines define hypertension as office BP >=140/90 mmHg.
title: Hypertension: Diagnosis and Treatment

text:
## Diagnosis and Measurement

- Patient seated and rested for 5 minutes
- Average of at least 2 readings taken 1-2 minutes apart
- Calibrated, validated sphygmomanometer with appropriate cuff size
- Confirm diagnosis with out-of-office measurements (ABPM or HBPM)
Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) is the gold standard,
capturing daytime average, nocturnal dipping, and BP variability. White-coat hypertension (office BP elevated, ABPM normal) occurs in
15-30% of patients. Masked hypertension (normal office BP, elevated ABPM)
carries the same cardiovascular risk as sustained hypertension. ## Secondary Hypertension
Secondary causes should be considered in patients with resistant
hypertension, age <30 years, or sudden onset.
title: Hypertension: Diagnosis and Treatment

text:
Common causes:
- Renovascular hypertension (renal artery stenosis)
- Primary aldosteronism (Conn syndrome): most common secondary cause (~10%)
- Phaeochromocytoma / paraganglioma
- Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA)
- Cushing syndrome
- Hypothyroidism / hyperthyroidism
- Coarctation of the aorta (young patients)
## Cardiovascular Risk Assessment
Total cardiovascular risk should guide treatment intensity. Risk calculators
include SCORE2 (European) and ASCVD Pooled Cohort Equations (US).
title: Hypertension: Diagnosis and Treatment

text:
Risk calculators
include SCORE2 (European) and ASCVD Pooled Cohort Equations (US). High-risk conditions warranting immediate treatment regardless of BP stage:
- Established CVD (coronary artery disease, stroke, PAD)
- Diabetes mellitus
- Chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage >=3
- LVEF <40%
## Treatment
### Lifestyle Modification
Non-pharmacological interventions are recommended for all patients:
- DASH diet: reduces systolic BP by 8-14 mmHg
- Sodium restriction (<2.3 g/day): reduces systolic BP by 5-6 mmHg
- Weight loss: 1 mmHg reduction per 1 kg weight loss
- Aerobic exercise (>=150 min/week moderate intensity)
- Alcohol limitation (<=14 units/week)
- Smoking cessation (does not lower BP but reduces overall CVD risk)
### Pharmacological Treatment
First-line antihypertensive agents (all reduce major cardiovascular events):
- Thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics: chlorthalidone 12.5-25 mg/day, indapamide 1.5-2.5 mg/day
- ACE inhibitors: ramipril 2.5-10 mg/day, perindopril 4-8 mg/day, enalapril 5-40 mg/day
- Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs): losartan 25-100 mg/day, olmesartan 10-40 mg/day
- Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (CCBs): amlodipine 2.5-10 mg/day, felodipine 2.5-10 mg/day
Combination therapy is required in most patients to achieve BP targets.
title: Hypertension: Diagnosis and Treatment

text:
Single-pill combinations (SPCs) improve adherence and are preferred. Triple therapy (RAS blocker + CCB + diuretic) achieves control in most patients. Resistant hypertension (BP uncontrolled on 3+ agents including a diuretic
at optimal doses) should prompt spironolactone 25-50 mg/day as a fourth agent,
or referral for specialist evaluation and investigation of secondary causes. ### BP Targets

with diabetes, CKD, CVD, or high CV risk. ESC/ESH 2018: initial target <140/90 mmHg; if tolerated, consider
<130/80 mmHg in most patients aged <65 years. ## Hypertensive Emergency
Hypertensive emergency: severe BP elevation (>180/120 mmHg) with acute
target organ damage (TOD). Examples include hypertensive encephalopathy,
acute coronary syndrome, acute aortic dissection, acute HF with pulmonary
oedema, and hypertensive nephrosclerosis. Management: IV antihypertensives in ICU setting.
title: Hypertension: Diagnosis and Treatment

text:
Management: IV antihypertensives in ICU setting. Reduce mean arterial
pressure (MAP) by no more than 25% in the first hour, then to 160/100-110
mmHg over 2-6 hours (except aortic dissection: target <120/80 mmHg urgently). Agents: IV labetalol, nicardipine, sodium nitroprusside, clevidipine.
title: Hypertension: Diagnosis and Treatment
